questions.prompt: Methane molecules have no permanent molecular dipole. Which model explains an attractive interaction between two CH4 molecules?
options: A permanent positive charge on one methane ion attracts a permanent negative charge on another.
Each methane molecule permanently aligns a C–H bond dipole with the net dipole of its neighbor.
A fluctuation in one electron cloud creates a temporary dipole that induces a correlated dipole in a neighboring molecule.
Dispersion attraction can occur only after a nearby ion permanently polarizes each methane molecule.
questions.explanation: C is correct. London dispersion interactions arise from temporary fluctuations and induced, correlated electron-cloud distortions. They occur even when molecules have no permanent dipoles, and also occur in polar species. A incorrectly treats neutral methane molecules as ions. B assumes a permanent molecular dipole despite methane’s symmetric cancellation of its bond dipoles. D incorrectly requires a pre-existing ion and permanent polarization; dispersion fluctuations do not require either. London dispersion is a specific interaction term; it should not be used as a synonym for every interaction sometimes grouped under van der Waals forces.

questions.prompt: Argon and xenon are both monatomic, nonpolar species. Why are dispersion interactions generally stronger between Xe atoms than between Ar atoms at comparable relative separations?
options: Xe has a larger electron cloud with more electrons, making it more readily polarized.
Xe has a permanent molecular dipole, whereas Ar does not.
Xe has a larger net positive charge, which attracts its neighbors more strongly.
Xe has fewer electrons, so its electron cloud is less shielded and cannot fluctuate.
questions.explanation: A is correct. Xenon’s larger, more electron-rich cloud is more polarizable, so correlated temporary dipoles can produce stronger dispersion interactions. B assigns a permanent dipole to an isolated spherical atom. C confuses greater nuclear charge with net atomic charge; both atoms are neutral overall. D reverses the electron-count comparison and incorrectly excludes fluctuations. Atomic or molecular mass can correlate with electron count within a series, but polarizability—not mass itself as an electrical charge—is the relevant microscopic idea.

questions.prompt: Two nonpolar C5H12 isomers have the same number of electrons. One has an extended chain shape; the other is compact and highly branched. Which prediction follows from the contact-area part of the dispersion model?
options: The compact isomer must form hydrogen bonds because branching increases the number of C–H bonds.
The extended isomer can have stronger net dispersion interactions because neighboring molecules can contact over a larger area.
The two isomers must have identical intermolecular interactions because their molecular formulas are identical.
The extended isomer has no dispersion interactions because its bonds are nonpolar.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Similar electron counts do not eliminate shape effects: extended molecules can provide more contact area for attractive dispersion interactions than compact isomers. A incorrectly infers an N–H, O–H, or F–H donor from branching; both isomers contain only C and H and have the same total C–H count. C ignores the geometry/contact-area contribution. D reverses the reason dispersion is important: nonpolar species still exhibit electron-cloud fluctuations. This is a qualitative interaction comparison, not an exact melting-point prediction.

questions.prompt: Pure dimethyl ether, CH3–O–CH3, is a polar molecular substance. In the usual AP intermolecular-force model, which interactions occur between its own molecules?
options: Only hydrogen bonding, because any molecule containing oxygen is a hydrogen-bond donor.
Only dispersion forces, because a molecule with no O–H bond cannot be polar.
Ion–dipole interactions, because every C–O bond creates a full O2- ion.
Dispersion and dipole–dipole interactions; it lacks an N–H, O–H, or F–H donor for self hydrogen bonding.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Polar ether molecules have permanent dipoles and all molecules have dispersion interactions. The ether oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond from a suitable different molecule, but pure dimethyl ether has no conventional N–H, O–H, or F–H donor. A confuses an oxygen acceptor with a donor. B confuses lack of a donor with lack of a molecular dipole. C turns covalent partial charges into full ions; intact ether molecules are neutral. The classification uses the stated introductory hydrogen-bonding convention.

questions.prompt: A methanol molecule, CH3–O–H, approaches a dimethyl ether molecule, CH3–O–CH3. Which contact can form a conventional hydrogen bond between these different molecules?
options: The carbon of methanol approaching a hydrogen bonded to carbon in the ether.
Any two carbon-bound hydrogens approaching, because all hydrogen atoms are hydrogen-bond donors.
The hydrogen on methanol’s O–H group pointing toward a lone-pair region on the ether oxygen.
The two oxygen ends point directly toward one another while methanol’s O–H hydrogen points away from the ether oxygen.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Methanol supplies an O–H donor and the ether oxygen supplies an acceptor lone-pair region. Both molecules need not contain O–H groups for a hydrogen bond between them. A lacks the required conventional donor–acceptor contact. B incorrectly treats C–H hydrogens as the usual AP N/O/F-bound donors. D places the two partially negative oxygen regions toward one another while the donor H points away; it lacks the stated favorable O–H···O donor–acceptor orientation. Dispersion and other dipolar interactions can also coexist; identifying this hydrogen bond does not remove them.

questions.prompt: A water molecule near a Na+ ion can rotate. Which orientation is favored by the ion–dipole interaction?
options: The partially positive H end points toward Na+, because all positive charges attract.
The partially negative O end points toward Na+.
Orientation has no effect because water is neutral overall.
Water must first split into H+ and OH- before an attractive orientation toward Na+ is possible.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Water’s oxygen end is partially negative and is attracted to the positive sodium ion. A reverses electrostatic attraction: bringing positive ends together is unfavorable. C ignores spatial separation of partial charges within a neutral polar molecule. D incorrectly requires covalent-bond cleavage and separate ions; intact polar water can interact with Na+. No covalent bond to Na+ or chemical transformation is needed to explain the favored orientation.

questions.prompt: An intact polar HCl molecule approaches a neutral Ar atom. In addition to dispersion, which interaction is expected in the introductory model?
options: Dipole-induced dipole, because HCl’s permanent dipole can distort Ar’s electron cloud.
Permanent dipole–permanent dipole, because a neutral Ar atom has a fixed positive and negative end.
Ion–dipole, because every HCl molecule must already be separate H+ and Cl- ions.
Conventional hydrogen bonding, because every molecule containing H forms such bonds with any neighbor.
questions.explanation: A is correct. A polar molecule can induce an electron-cloud distortion in a nonpolar neighbor, producing a dipole-induced dipole attraction. B incorrectly assigns a permanent dipole to isolated Ar. C contradicts the specified intact HCl molecule; its covalent partial charges are not separate full ions here. D ignores the conventional N/O/F donor and acceptor requirements and supplies no suitable acceptor on Ar. The induced interaction occurs without permanent ion formation.

questions.prompt: Consider two arrangements of the same pair of HCl molecules at comparable center-to-center separation. In I, one molecule’s partially positive H end points toward the other’s partially negative Cl end. In II, the two partially positive H ends point toward each other. Which dipole-based comparison is appropriate?
options: II is favored because like partial charges attract one another.
The arrangements must have equal interaction energies because each molecule has the same dipole magnitude in both.
I is favored because unlike partial charges face one another; relative orientation matters as well as dipole magnitude.
Neither arrangement can have an intermolecular interaction because both molecules are neutral.
questions.explanation: C is correct. The head-to-tail arrangement places unlike partial charges near one another, giving a favorable dipole alignment. A reverses the charge-attraction rule. B omits orientation from a dipole–dipole comparison; equal dipole magnitudes do not imply equal interaction energies at different orientations. D confuses net neutrality with absence of local partial charges or dispersion. The comparison isolates the stated geometries and comparable separations; it does not claim that molecules in a liquid remain permanently frozen in one orientation.

questions.prompt: A student argues that any small polar molecule must have stronger net intermolecular attractions than every large nonpolar molecule. Which response best evaluates that claim?
options: The claim is correct because dispersion forces vanish whenever a permanent dipole is absent.
The claim is correct because a permanent dipole always dominates every possible dispersion interaction.
The claim is incorrect because polar molecules have only dispersion forces and no dipole–dipole interactions.
The claim is too broad: a large, highly polarizable nonpolar molecule can have stronger net intermolecular attractions than a small polar species because of substantial dispersion interactions.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Interaction strength depends on polarizability, contact area, dipoles, and geometry. Dispersion can dominate the net attractions of large species; there is no universal ranking that ignores size and structure. A reverses the existence of dispersion in nonpolar species. B makes the unsupported absolute assertion that any permanent dipole outweighs every dispersion contribution. C incorrectly removes the additional dipole–dipole interactions of polar species. A comparison must consider the actual molecules rather than just their polar/nonpolar labels.

questions.prompt: Two distant regions of one large biomolecule approach during folding. One region has an O–H group and another has a carbonyl oxygen with an available lone-pair region. No covalent bonds are changed. Which statement is consistent with the intermolecular/interparticle model?
options: A hydrogen-bond contact between these regions can stabilize the folded arrangement, even though both regions belong to the same molecule.
Hydrogen bonding is impossible because it can occur only between separate molecules.
The contact must create a new O–O covalent bond and remove the O–H bond.
The carbonyl oxygen cannot be an acceptor because it is already bonded to carbon.
questions.explanation: A is correct. Conventional hydrogen bonding can occur between different molecules or between appropriate regions of one large molecule. An O–H donor can interact with a carbonyl-O acceptor without changing covalent connectivity. B wrongly excludes intramolecular contacts. C changes covalent bonds contrary to the stated scenario and the noncovalent model. D confuses being covalently bonded with lacking available lone pairs; carbonyl oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond. The question says the contact can stabilize this arrangement, not that one contact alone determines all folding energetics.

questions.prompt: A simplified comparison holds the separation, orientation, and polarizability of a nonpolar partner constant. The permanent dipole magnitude of its polar partner is increased. What happens to the dipole-induced dipole attraction in this model?
options: It becomes weaker because a larger permanent dipole prevents electron-cloud distortion.
It becomes stronger because the larger permanent dipole induces a larger distortion in the polarizable partner.
It becomes repulsive because induced dipoles always oppose attractive interactions.
It remains identical because only permanent dipole–permanent dipole interactions depend on dipole magnitude.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Holding the nonpolar partner and geometry fixed, a stronger polar field produces a greater induced dipole and a stronger attractive induced interaction. A reverses the field-distortion relationship. C confuses the induced charge arrangement with an inherently repulsive force; the induced arrangement is attractive in this model. D omits a central dependence of dipole-induced dipole strength. This constrained comparison does not assert that changing a real molecule leaves every other interaction or geometry unchanged.
